power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

In the past decade, the rapid advancement of information and communications technology (ICT) has made telehealth an important tool for managing health and wellness, especially for those living in remote areas or with limited access to healthcare services.
The COVID-19 pandemic has further accelerated its widespread adoption [1].
text.formatted: The COVID-19 pandemic has further accelerated its widespread adoption <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Telehealth is a broad term that encompasses the remote delivery of health-related services by healthcare professionals.

Specifically, tele-exercise refers to the remote delivery of home-based exercise interventions through video-linked appointments using videoconferencing software like Zoom, Skype, FaceTime, or VooV, along with devices such as smartphones, tablets, or computers equipped with webcams and internet connections [2].
text.formatted: Specifically, tele-exercise refers to the remote delivery of home-based exercise interventions through video-linked appointments using videoconferencing software like Zoom, Skype, FaceTime, or VooV, along with devices such as smartphones, tablets, or computers equipped with webcams and internet connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: The effective adoption of tele-exercise offers significant potential to enhance care continuity, improve individual access, and bypass traditional logistical barriers such as travel and adverse weather, which is particularly beneficial for community-dwelling older adults at risk of falls [3, 4].
text.formatted: The effective adoption of tele-exercise offers significant potential to enhance care continuity, improve individual access, and bypass traditional logistical barriers such as travel and adverse weather, which is particularly beneficial for community-dwelling older adults at risk of falls <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Recent systematic reviews demonstrate that tele-exercise can achieve clinical outcomes comparable to traditional f2f interventions [5].
text.formatted: Recent systematic reviews demonstrate that tele-exercise can achieve clinical outcomes comparable to traditional f2f interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, qualitative studies exploring the acceptability of recreation-and rehabilitation-oriented tele-exercise reveal that while older adults appreciate the convenience of home delivery, they frequently encounter initial technological barriers [6] [7] [8].
text.formatted: Furthermore, qualitative studies exploring the acceptability of recreation-and rehabilitation-oriented tele-exercise reveal that while older adults appreciate the convenience of home delivery, they frequently encounter initial technological barriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Many older adults experience digital exclusion or 'tech fear', though they can gradually adapt with adequate external support.

However, while previous literature successfully describes these subjective barriers, it often fails to systematically translate these lived experiences into actionable, theory-driven strategies for intervention design.

Consequently, less attention has been given to the precise mechanisms required to facilitate the behavioural transition from a preference for traditional f2f classes to sustained engagement in a digital modality.

To understand how tele-exercise can be effectively embedded into community care, it is necessary to move beyond simply identifying barriers and toward an in-depth behavioural diagnosis of the individual, social, and environmental factors influencing uptake.

Recent research highlights that tailored implementation strategies are crucial for improving the uptake of falls prevention recommendations in practice [9] The Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) provides a comprehensive framework for this translation [10].
text.formatted: Recent research highlights that tailored implementation strategies are crucial for improving the uptake of falls prevention recommendations in practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> The Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) provides a comprehensive framework for this translation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: At its core, the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) model acts as a behavioural system, positing that engagement requires adequate Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation.
The Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) expands this by subdividing the components into granular domains, allowing for a precise analysis of the theoretical mechanisms at play [11].
text.formatted: The Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) expands this by subdividing the components into granular domains, allowing for a precise analysis of the theoretical mechanisms at play <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, these diagnostic domains can then be mapped to the Behaviour Change Technique Taxonomy v1 (BCTTv1), which provides the specific "active ingredients" (e.g., graded tasks, practical social support) needed to directly target identified deficits [10].
text.formatted: Crucially, these diagnostic domains can then be mapped to the Behaviour Change Technique Taxonomy v1 (BCTTv1), which provides the specific "active ingredients" (e.g., graded tasks, practical social support) needed to directly target identified deficits <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the aim of this study was to qualitatively explore the experiences and perceptions of community-dwelling older adults at risk of falls who participated in a synchronous teleexercise programme.

By utilising the COM-B model and TDF as theoretical lenses, this study sought to identify the precise determinants and facilitating factors influencing the engagement and uptake of this novel delivery mode.

Furthermore, by linking these theoretical domains to specific BCTs, this research aims to provide actionable recommendations for designing future, multi-option tele-exercise frameworks that effectively foster sustained physical activity behaviour change in aging populations.
The study was nested within a RCT comparing synchronous group-based tele-exercise (TE) versus community-based (CB) exercise for older adults at risk of falls.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the first author's institution (RC/ETH/H/0029).
The study was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2200063370) on 5 September 2022.
The study protocol has been published [12], with quantitative results under review [13].
text.formatted: The study protocol has been published <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, with quantitative results under review <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Preliminary descriptive findings from this dataset were previously presented as a conference abstract [14].
text.formatted: Preliminary descriptive findings from this dataset were previously presented as a conference abstract <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: This manuscript reanalyses qualitative data, mapping to COM-B, TDF, and BCTs to inform intervention design.
The intervention was a modified Otago Exercise Programme (OEP) delivered over three months.
TE sessions were held via Zoom in participants' homes, with devices provided as needed.
All participants attended thrice-weekly, 45-minute classes (8-11 per group).
Sessions followed a structured format-warm-up, OEP [15], "workouts on demand," cool-down-led by an instructor in their late 60s experienced with teaching older adults.
text.formatted: Sessions followed a structured format-warm-up, OEP <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, "workouts on demand," cool-down-led by an instructor in their late 60s experienced with teaching older adults.

text.text: Exercises were tailored (e.g., shorter holds, fewer reps for low strength), with individual feedback during and after sessions [12].
text.formatted: Exercises were tailored (e.g., shorter holds, fewer reps for low strength), with individual feedback during and after sessions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: This qualitative study used semi-structured interviews to explore barriers and enablers of teleexercise training in older adults at risk of falls.
Analysis was guided by the TDF and the COM-B model.

The TDF consolidates constructs from multiple behaviour change theories into 14 domains (e.g. knowledge, skills, role, self-efficacy, environment) [16], mapped onto COM-B's components: Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation [17].
text.formatted: The TDF consolidates constructs from multiple behaviour change theories into 14 domains (e.g. knowledge, skills, role, self-efficacy, environment) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, mapped onto COM-B's components: Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Written informed consent was obtained before semi-structured interviews, conducted March-July 2023 either f2f in community centres or via Zoom, depending on preference.
All sessions were held privately to ensure confidentiality.
Interviews were conducted by the researcher 1 (MSc, male) and researcher 2 (PhD, female), trained by researcher 3 (PhD, female), an experienced qualitative researcher.
No prior relationship existed; participants only knew the team as academic investigators delivering and evaluating the tele-exercise programme.
A semi-structured guide, based on TDF domains and literature [21, 22], was pilot-tested with four participants (supplementary material S1).

Theme search: Inductive codes were grouped into sub-themes within COM-B/TDF categories.
Theme review: Themes were cross-checked against data; discrepancies resolved through consensus until 100% agreement.

Six themes were identified to describe the tele-exercise experiences of older adults at risk of falls and to identify the behavioural mechanisms influencing their engagement.

These themes were: (1) technological skills, access, and support; (2) coach support and exercise adaptability; (3) health motivation and goal achievement; (4) emotional journey with technology; (5) home environment and accessibility; and (6) social interaction dynamics.

These themes and their behavioural mechanisms were mapped onto the COM-B model and TDF domains (Table 3) and operationalised into BCW intervention functions, active BCTTv1 ingredients, and future recommendations (Fig 1, Supplementary material S4 ).

Sub-theme: Barriers -Technological Limitations Affecting Participation For a cohort where 52% had primary education or below, unfamiliarity with digital devices represented an initial deficit in Psychological Capability (COM-B).

P1 (age 90-94, Edu 1, attendance 97.2%, PACES 100) noted that the fear of making irreversible errors induced immediate apprehension: "At first, it might be intimidating if you don't understand, but once you do, there's no need to worry.
If you don't know how, you might mess things up."
This hesitation acted as a cognitive gatekeeper before physical exercise began.

Lacking environmental scaffolding (COM-B: Physical Opportunity), minor glitches provoked acute helplessness, enforcing dependency on younger relatives: "We older folks tend to be a bit scared of new technology.
If something goes wrong, we don't know how to fix it, so we have to ask younger people for help" (P9, age 70-74, Edu 4, attendance 55.6%, PACES 101).
Hardware and connectivity constraints further restricted Physical Opportunity (COM-B).
P2 (age 70-74, Edu 5, attendance 91.7%, PACES 120) described environmental instability in rural village housing, where poor broadband weakened reception and disrupted exercise routines.
Crucially, small tablet displays created safety-critical barriers to motor skill acquisition (TDF: Skills): "The screen is too small.
When we're doing the exercises, it's hard to see the coach's little movements... like when he raises his heel a little bit" (P3, age 75-79, Edu 2, attendance 94.4%, PACES 116).
Inability to discern subtle postural adjustments heightened fall anxiety during unspotted home training.

Hands-on onboarding by the research team provided vital cognitive scaffolding, restoring Psychological Capability (COM-B) through step-by-step demonstration (BCT 6.1), guided rehearsal (BCT 8.1), and practical social support (BCT 3.2).
P5 (age 80-84, Edu 1, attendance 66.7%, PACES 95) shared: "I know how to turn on the computer tablet, but I have trouble with the devices.
But you guys taught me how to adjust the volume on the speakers, right?
And turning on... and using the tablet are pretty much the same as turning it off."
Mastering basic operations generated an immediate surge in Beliefs about Capabilities (TDF): "The difficulty was at the beginning...
You guys showed me how to do it.
It's much better now" (P8, age 75-79, Edu 4, attendance 86.1%, PACES 120).
Rapid technical troubleshooting functioned as essential Social Opportunity (COM-B), mitigating transient tech-anxiety (TDF: Emotion).

Support ranged from optimizing audio amplification (P1) to resolving live connection failures: "Even if sometimes I feel anxious and can't log into the class... you quickly found a reason for it... addressing the problems right away" (P18, age 75-79, Edu 4, attendance 86.1%, PACES 106).
Prompt resolution absorbed the emotional burden of technical failure, allowing participants to reserve cognitive capacity for physical training.
The virtual interface diminished the immediacy of f2f interaction, creating safety concerns and weakening behavioural reinforcement.
P5 described feeling invisible: "(Talking to the coach, you wonder if he can hear you) I've never said anything before, because he's never called my name."
This perceived absence of verbal acknowledgment undermined Social Opportunity (COM-B) and Reflective Motivation, rendering participants passive viewers.

Furthermore, latency in error correction disrupted real-time feedback loops essential for safe balance acquisition (TDF: Skills, Environmental Context and Resources): "In a physical class, the instructor would respond immediately.
However, in a computer-based environment, the response wouldn't be instantaneous" (P12, age 75-79, Edu 2, attendance 80.6%, PACES 103).
The coach's adaptive instruction bridged the physical distance, serving as the primary catalyst for self-efficacy.
By offering regressed movements, coaches utilized Graded Tasks (BCT 8.
Synchronous coaching provided continuous visual modelling (TDF: Social Influences), stimulating Automatic and Reflective Motivation (COM-B): "the coach explains everything so clearly.
When he demonstrates, it's really clear...
The coach does it with you, so it motivates you to do it" (P3).
P2 highlighted the value of percentage-based effort scaling: "The coach also adjusts the exercises...
'Just do 70% or 60% of it, that's enough.'
I was a bit nervous at first, but I realized later that this course is pretty suitable and... gradual."

Scaling exertion to 60-70% capacity (BCT 8.7) provided psychological safety, downregulating negative affective arousal (TDF: Emotion) and turning performance apprehension into attainable routine (TDF: Beliefs about Capabilities).
Sub-theme: Barriers -Movement Challenges Linked to Health Conditions Pre-existing musculoskeletal impairments exposed baseline deficits in Physical Capability (COM-B) and motor stamina (TDF: Skills).
P9 noted that repeated unilateral movements aggravated left foot weakness ("repeat the same movement three or four times... makes it a bit harder"), while P12 admitted: "I stop when he stops.
But it's really tough.
I mean, my legs just aren't strong enough."
P24 (age 70-74, Edu 4, attendance 80.6%, PACES 120) explicitly linked balance deficits to fall-related fear: "Balance is the hardest thing...
Some movements are just too hard for me...
My balance is really bad."
These deficits emphasise that balance interventions in frail cohorts require carefully curated biomechanical loads to prevent injury and disengagement.
Tangible physiological improvements acted as powerful operant conditioning (TDF: Reinforcement), strengthening Reflective Motivation (COM-B).
Enhanced muscle tone directly reduced kinesiophobia: "I can tell my thigh muscles are a lot more toned now.
That gives me more confidence going downstairs, so I'm not scared of tripping forward anymore" (P3).
For P22 (age 75-79, Edu 3, attendance 94.4%, PACES 113), relief from chronic back pain served as a somatic reward, transforming exercise from a chore into a daily selfmanagement ritual.

Participants also reported cognitive restructuring regarding aging: "Whether it's thinking, memory, or bodily functions, I feel healthier, and the decline seems to slow down... exercising is very positive for me" (P3).
Functional recovery fostered behavioural spillover into recreational life: "My legs are stronger now!
I went to play ping pong... my legs didn't feel as tired...
I even walk faster now" (P16, age 65-69, Edu 2, attendance 94.4%, PACES 96).

Finally, predictable scheduling (Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays at 11:00 AM; P2, P3) reduced cognitive load, acting as an environmental prompt (TDF: Behavioural Regulation) that converted effortful intention into Automatic Motivation (COM-B) driven by habit.

Unfamiliarity with technology initially triggered passive avoidance and learned helplessness, reflecting a collapse of Reflective Motivation (COM-B) and low Beliefs about Capabilities (TDF): "I don't know how to press it, so I'll just let it be.
There's nothing else you can do; you just have to sit there and wait" (P13, age 85-89, Edu 1, attendance 69.4%, PACES 104).

P18 voiced acute anxiety regarding compromised autonomy and family reliance (COM-B: Social Opportunity): "My biggest worry is that if something unexpected happens during class, I won't know which button to press.
My daughter might not be there to help."
Exercising in congested living quarters restricted range of motion and elevated collision hazards: "There are many things at home, and my family buys a lot of stuff.
There's little space, and the bed is filled with food" (P1).

Conflicting family routines introduced competing social demands (COM-B: Social Opportunity; P2), while afternoon sunlight glare disrupted visual tracking (TDF: Environmental Context and Resources): "There's glare -the sun from the west causes a lot of reflection" (P20, age 70-74, Edu 2, attendance 91.7%, PACES 112), forcing participants to guess postures and introducing balance risks.
Eliminating transit burdens conserved limited Physical Capability (COM-B), especially for seniors requiring walking aids: "I don't want to go to the centre's exercise class every day.
I have to walk on a slope and use my cane" (P1).
Removing the logistical exhaustion of commuting lowered behavioural friction: "When I go to the centre, I have to rush there half an hour early.
But here, I just turn on the tablet first... and when it's time, I just step over and join in" (P5).
This frictionless transition anchored the routine within the home environment (TDF: Environmental Context and Resources; COM-B: Physical Opportunity).
Domestic environments blurred classroom boundaries; ambient noise and background televisions from unmuted homes disrupted group focus (COM-B: Social Opportunity; P9).
Furthermore, internalized cultural norms of deference toward the instructor suppressed spontaneous horizontal peer communication (TDF: Social Influences): "It's class, and that's the coach!
It's disrespectful to chat while the coach is teaching.
You can't just pretend the coach isn't there!"
(P25, age 65-69, Edu 4, attendance 72.2%, PACES 106).

text.text: Offline Community Re-anchoring: Rather than forcing online socialization, tele-exercise served as a common ground for peer interaction deferred to community centre visits (COM-B: Social Opportunity; TDF: Reinforcement; P4).
P4 shared that ""I am happier now because I have learned something, and we get to interact with each other (after class in the community centre)."

Preserving Cognitive-Motor Focus: Other participants actively preferred virtual separation to eliminate social distractions and preserve cognitive bandwidth (TDF: Memory, Attention, and Decision Processes): "Once the online exercise class is over, that's it, but communication... isn't that important" (P17, age 75-79, Edu 4, attendance 94.4%, PACES 121).

P22 (age 75-79, Edu 3, attendance 94.4%, PACES 113) emphasised that avoiding conversational obligations was necessary to maintain balance: "I'm worried that after you get familiar with them, they might come over and chat...
They're not exercising, just talking...
I really like to focus."
Preferences for exercise training format were coded into three categories (f2f, online, no preference) and analysed quantitatively using frequency counts.
The majority preferred in-person classes as a psychological safety net.

Immediate error correction transferred the burden of safety back to the expert (TDF: Reinforcement, Skills): "If I make a mistake, the coach will know right away and correct us immediately" (P6, age 65-69, Edu 2, attendance 100%, PACES 119).
Multi-sensory instruction bridged educational gaps: "You can actually touch and feel things, which is clearer than online" (P8).

Additionally, physical attendance provided essential Social Opportunity (COM-B) and emotional co-regulation (TDF: Emotion), counteracting chronic loneliness among solitary seniors: "Having someone to talk to is important.
It allows everyone to check in on each other and feel less lonely" (P9; supported by P15).
A focused minority favoured remote classes for visual and cognitive efficiency.

Digital camera zoom provided clearer instructional demonstrations than crowded community halls (TDF: Social Influences): "Because there are fewer people, I can get a close-up view of what the instructor is doing" (P22).

Minimizing social chatter lowered cognitive dual-task demands, allowing undivided attention on balance execution (TDF: Attention, Decision Making, and Memory): "In a real-life class, there are too many people talking, and it's harder to focus" (P23, age 80-84, Edu 1, attendance 97.2%, PACES 114).
P24 highlighted personal autonomy: "Once you log off, everyone can go do their own things... online feels like it's just me and the coach" (TDF: Behavioural Regulation).

Over a quarter expressed situational ambivalence, treating the modalities as complementary: • Environmental & Weather Resilience: Home sessions protected routine adherence during adverse weather (TDF: Environmental Context and Resources): "Even if it's freezing cold or raining, you can still exercise at home" (P2).

• Perceived Instructional Equivalence: Highly adapted participants experienced no communication deficits: "You can call out to him, and they'll hear you right away, just like f2f" (P10, age 65-69, Edu 2, attendance 86.1%, PACES 102).
This study applied the COM B model and TDF to examine older adults' engagement in synchronous tele exercise.
Key determinants were identified among those facing a "double barrier"-risk of falls combined with lower socioeconomic status and limited technology access.
By mapping sub themes to theoretical domains and specific BCTs, the findings yield actionable strategies for designing tele exercise programmes that can be embedded within community care systems.
In prior literature, technical issues are framed as operational hurdles [26].

text.text: For older adults at high fall risk living alone, however, these challenges became safety-critical.
With 52% having only primary education, navigation errors often led to acute helplessness (P13; Theme 4).
Lacking co-residing family, participants feared misinterpreting cues or audio lags during balance drills could trigger unmonitored falls, undermining Psychological Capability.
Anxiety was mitigated not by practice alone but through coach-mediated adaptability (Theme 2).
Calibrated exertion targets (e.g., 60-70% effort, seated variations; P2) provided mastery experiences and verbal persuasion, restoring Beliefs about Capabilities.
This structured support offered psychological safety while maintaining physical challenge, consistent with Self-Efficacy Theory [27].

Remote delivery reduced barriers such as transport and adverse weather [28], especially for mobility-compromised seniors navigating slopes and stairs (P1).

text.text: Tele-exercise thus provides a safe, adaptive alternative when travel is hazardous, provided remote coaching scaffolds both physical and psychological safety.
A primary strength of this study lies in its systematic, theory-driven design pipeline spanning the TDF [36], the COM-B model, the BCW [17], and the BCTTv1 [24].

Mapping these determinants into COM-B and cross-referencing with BCW functions established a logic model, while appraisal against APEASE (Affordability, Practicability, Effectiveness, Acceptability, Side-effects, and Equity) criteria safeguarded feasibility and equity.

Recommendations emphasise higher-order BCTs: proactive Action planning (1.4), Restructuring the physical environment (12.1), and Restructuring the social environment (12.2).

text.text: Integrating these structural BCTs elevates tele-exercise from remote clinical adaptation to a resilient, context-aware complex intervention.

A major strength of this study is its use of the COM-B model and TDF to explain teleexercise adoption, translating qualitative insights into actionable BCTs and offering scalable guidance for digital health.

It also captures the experiences of a vulnerable group-older adults with high fall risk, low education, and high rates of living alone (52%)-showing that digital exclusion can be mitigated through targeted support.

Limitations include a socio-demographically homogenous sample (single ethnicity, 80% female), restricting generalisability, and high attendance (85.5%) and enjoyment (PACES), which may reflect selection bias.

The coupon, though ethically intended as compensation, may have introduced minor volunteer bias and social desirability bias. participants who volunteered and remained engaged were likely more motivated and health-conscious than the broader older adult population.
To reduce these risks, participants were assured that compensation was guaranteed regardless of feedback and encouraged to provide critical views.

This study shows tele-exercise is feasible and acceptable for community-dwelling older adults at risk of falls, challenging assumptions that low digital literacy or socioeconomic barriers preclude digital health adoption.
Using the COM-B model and TDF, it demonstrates that technology-related anxiety and physical limitations can be mitigated through targeted BCTs.
Mastery of the technology shifted emotions from anxiety to pride, reinforcing digital self-efficacy.
Despite high adherence and enjoyment, over half preferred f2f delivery, indicating that format preference does not dictate engagement.
To ensure safety and engagement, future programmes should embed identified BCTs within a structured framework.
Addressing structural and psychological barriers can strengthen self-efficacy and sustain remote participation, offering a practical pathway to active ageing.
